transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-03-15
Start: 14:00 PT
Duration: 48 minutes (recorded)
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lin Chen (Redwood SE), Rachel Kim (Aurora CTO), Marcus Lee (Aurora Head of Platform), Dina Santos (Aurora SRE)
Meeting ID: ff-20280315-aurora-001
Artifacts: Redwood reliability deck (link), sample SLA doc (to be shared)

[00:00] Samir: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. Uh, can we do quick intros? I'm Samir Patel, I'm the AE covering payments and infra. Lin's our solutions engineer.
[00:12] Rachel: Hey Samir, Rachel here, CTO at Aurora. We run payment orchestration, global rails, lots of low-latency requirements.
[00:18] Marcus: Marcus, head of platform. We own networking, infra, incident response, et cetera.
[00:22] Dina: Dina, SRE, I manage uptime and on-call for our inference services.
[00:26] Lin: Lin Chen, SE at Redwood, I focus on serving runtime, routing, and fallbacks.
[00:30] Samir: Great. Objective for today is to understand Aurora's reliability and incident tolerance needs for LLM-powered features and talk through Redwood options: Hosted, Dedicated, Private and how we do multi-region and fallback policies.

[02:10] Rachel: High level — we have customers in EU, NA, APAC. Latency under 200ms is ideal for auth flows, for batch risk checks we can tolerate higher. Primary concerns: region failover, data residency, and predictable tail latency during incidents.
[02:45] Marcus: Also want to avoid single-region blast radius; if one cloud region has issues we need automated routing to another region with minimal manual steps.
[03:03] Dina: And auditability — need logs, KMS integrations, RBAC, and to know what falls back where.

[04:15] Lin: Right. At a high level Redwood supports a couple of patterns: active-active multi-region routing where requests go to nearest region with health checks, and active-passive with automated failover. We also have model-variant fallbacks — e.g., if the high-accuracy model is unavailable we route to a compatible, lower-cost or quantized variant.
[04:45] Rachel: How seamless is that switch? Does it change tokenization or output shape? We need deterministic behavior for certain flows.
[05:05] Lin: Good question — there are two levers. For structured outputs we recommend model variants that preserve output schema; small differences in wording can happen, but we can tie regressions to prompt sets. For critical flows we do canarying and deterministic rollbacks.

[06:20] Marcus: When you say health checks, what's the detection window? We can't have long failover windows.
[06:30] Lin: Health checks are configurable. Default probe interval is 10s with baked-in circuit breaker logic — after N consecutive failures we start rerouting. For customer-configurable SLOs we tune thresholds; e.g., aggressive failover can be within 20-30s, but you pay with some risk of false positives.

[07:10] Dina: If we failover to a different region, what about data residency / logs? We can't leak EU data to other jurisdictions.
[07:20] Samir: For Hosted we support region pinning and routing policies — you can say EU-only for PII-sensitive requests. For Private (VPC/on-prem) you keep control with customer-managed KMS and local audit logs. Dedicated reserved capacity can be provisioned per region to meet residency constraints.
[07:40] Rachel: Ok. What's the SLA for Hosted vs Dedicated?
[07:48] Samir: Our standard Hosted SLA for paid customers is 99.9% for model endpoints, with latency SLOs per model-profile. Dedicated has higher guarantees — 99.95 uptime, and we can offer enterprise SLA add-ons for 99.99 depending on commit. Private is by negotiation. I will send the formal SLA doc.

[09:05] Marcus: Can you describe fallback tiers? For example, primary model on GPU, then quantized CPU fallback, then a cached response?
[09:18] Lin: Exactly. We typically recommend a 3-tier fallback chain: 1) Primary high-accuracy GPU model (hosted/dedicated), 2) Quantized model variant (reduced precision) that runs on cheaper instances with slightly higher latency, 3) Cached prefix or templated fallback for extremely degraded scenarios. You can also route to a synchronous non-LLM rule engine as last resort.
[09:50] Dina: How do you monitor quality regression when fallback happens? We can't silently degrade without detection.
[09:58] Lin: Redwood Optimize can run continuous evals against golden prompt sets. We trigger alerts if failure-mode outputs deviate beyond thresholds. We attach request-level labels so you can slice by route/region/model and track regression rates.

[11:12] Rachel: About rollout strategies — we need canarying and automatic rollback if latency or error rate spikes.
[11:20] Lin: We support canary deployments with traffic percentage splits and automated rollback rules (error rate > X or P99 latency > Y). Rollouts can be route-based, user-segment-based, or tenant-based.

[12:40] Marcus: Network-wise, if one cloud provider has an outage, does Redwood router switch providers or just regions within the same provider?
[12:50] Samir: Both. If you're on Hosted we have multi-cloud presence and can route across providers; for Dedicated we can set up cross-cloud pools but that's part of the infra design. Private customers can use our control plane to orchestrate failovers between on-prem and cloud endpoints.

[14:05] Dina: Encryption at rest/in transit and KMS — we need HSM-backed KMS, logs that are tamper-evident.
[14:15] Samir: We integrate with customer KMS (Cloud KMS, HSM) for Private and Dedicated. Hosted can support customer-managed keys for enterprise accounts. Audit logs are exportable to Splunk/Datadog and we provide append-only log shipping options for compliance.

[16:30] Rachel: Let's talk about costs during failover. If we route to a more expensive region or spin up dedicated nodes, how is that charged?
[16:40] Samir: Failover compute is charged per-used tokens/compute as normal; Dedicated reserved capacity handles spikes within committed capacity. For sudden cross-region bursts you might see higher egress or instance costs — we can set cost-based routing rules to prefer cheaper region unless health degrades.

[18:00] Marcus: Can we set a policy like: prefer EU region for EU traffic, but if EU region P99 latency > 300ms or error rate > 1% route to NA?
[18:10] Lin: Yes, that's a common policy. Policies are rule-driven and can be layered: geo-preference, health thresholds, cost thresholds, and user-tier overrides.

[20:05] Rachel: For pilot, we'd like two routes: 1) Auth flow (low-latency, EU primary), 2) Risk scoring (batched, global). Can Redwood support different fallback chains per route?
[20:18] Samir: Absolutely. Each route has its own model set, cache policy, batching config, and fallback chain. We'll provision a Dedicated pool in EU for auth in the pilot and a global hosted route for risk scoring.

[23:30] Dina: What's telemetry look like during incidents? We need traces, token-level cost breakdown, per-request model variant info.
[23:40] Lin: Console provides per-route dashboards, tracing hooks, and token-level cost/latency. During incidents you can open a support escalation and we provide a (SLA dependent) incident runbook and war-room support.

[26:02] Rachel: A few operational questions: how fast can Dedicated capacity scale? Can you burst cross-region?
[26:12] Samir: Autoscaling configs are flexible. Dedicated pools can autoscale but there's a lead time for cold capacity depending on hardware; we also support burst capacity options (hot spare pools) for critical clients. Cross-region bursts require pre-provisioned capacity or using Hosted fallback.

[30:00] Marcus: Are there known gotchas with KV cache or prefix caching during region failover?
[30:10] Lin: Yes — cache locality matters. On failover you may see cache misses, which transiently increases latency. We recommend warming strategies and shared cache for certain keys or accepting a brief cold-cache window during failover. We sometimes see transcripts where KV cache was transcribed as KV "cash" in our older notes — ha — transcription quirks aside.

[33:40] Rachel: Security checklist — SOC2, ISO, SAML/SSO, RBAC, SIEM integration, KMS, data deletion policies?
[33:50] Samir: We are SOC2 and ISO cert'd (enterprise package). We support SSO with SAML/OIDC, RBAC at route/model level, and SIEM integrations. I'll attach the security pack.

[36:10] Dina: One more: during a rollout can we set an automatic fallback to a rule-engine for N% of requests if model returns errors?
[36:20] Lin: Yes, we have fallback chains that can include non-LLM services as a final step. You can define percentage thresholds, e.g., 5% to rule engine while we investigate.

[40:00] Samir: Ok, to recap: Redwood can support multi-region routing, model-variant fallbacks, per-route policies, and enterprise SLAs. We'll share SLA/security docs and an architecture diagram. Pilot: two routes (auth + risk) with Dedicated EU pool for auth, Hosted global for risk, measurement period 1 week.
[40:28] Rachel: Sounds good. We'll send traffic profiles and list of golden prompts for evals.
[40:35] Marcus: We'll want a pre-kickoff tech read with our infra team to reconcile subnet/VPC peering and peering configs.
[40:42] Dina: I'll compile the security questionnaire items we need answered.
[41:00] Samir: Great — action items and deadlines in the notes. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up by email with the docs and a proposed pilot schedule.
[41:12] Rachel: Thanks, bye.

(ends at ~14:48 PT, 48 minutes recorded)
